questions.question: What are Pods, Deployments, Services, and ConfigMaps in Kubernetes and how do they relate?
questions.title: Kubernetes Core Objects: Pod, Deployment, Service, ConfigMap
questions.direct_answer: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit (one or more containers sharing network/storage). A Deployment manages Pod replicas declaratively with rolling updates and rollbacks. A Service provides a stable network endpoint to a dynamic set of Pods. A ConfigMap stores non-sensitive configuration data as key-value pairs injected into Pods as env vars or files.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the Kubernetes abstraction hierarchy and why each object exists
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking a Pod and a container are the same thing, or not knowing why Deployments are used instead of managing Pods directly (Deployments provide self-healing and rollout management)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the controller reconciliation loop — Deployment controller continuously reconciles desired state with actual state, ReplicaSet ensures pod count, and mention how Services use label selectors to discover Pods dynamically

sections.title: The Misconception That Costs You the Interview: Pods Are Not Containers
sections.content:
Most developers first learning Kubernetes assume that a Pod is just another name for a container. That assumption breaks the moment they try to run a sidecar proxy alongside their Spring Boot app — both containers must share a network namespace and lifecycle, and that shared boundary is the Pod. Understanding the four core objects — Pod, Deployment, Service, ConfigMap — as layers of abstraction rather than standalone things is what separates a developer who uses `kubectl` from one who understands what it does.

**A Pod wraps one or more containers** into a single scheduling unit. Containers in the same Pod share `localhost` networking and can mount the same volumes. They start and stop together. But Pods are ephemeral — when a node fails, the Pod is gone forever. Nobody recreates it automatically unless a controller is watching.

The real question interviewers are probing: why do these four objects exist as separate abstractions instead of one monolithic resource? The answer is separation of concerns. Each object owns exactly one responsibility, and they compose through **label selectors** — the same labeling mechanism that a Deployment uses to own its Pods is the mechanism a Service uses to route traffic to them.

sections.title: The Controller Loop That Makes Deployments Self-Healing
sections.content:
The Deployment controller watches the Kubernetes API server in a continuous **reconciliation loop**: compare desired state (3 replicas running image v2.1) with actual state (2 pods running, 1 crashed), then take action (create 1 replacement pod). This loop runs constantly, not just at deploy time.

When you create a Deployment, it does not directly manage Pods. It creates a **ReplicaSet** — an intermediate object whose only job is maintaining the desired number of identical Pod replicas. The Deployment manages ReplicaSets, and ReplicaSets manage Pods. This two-layer indirection exists for rolling updates: when you change the image tag, the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet for the new version and scales down the old one, keeping both alive during the transition.

This is the insight interviewers want to hear. Pods crash, nodes fail, resources get preempted — none of that requires human intervention because the controller loop detects the drift and corrects it automatically. A ConfigMap follows a different pattern entirely: it stores non-sensitive configuration as key-value pairs that Pods reference, but it has no controller loop of its own. Updating a ConfigMap does not trigger a Pod restart unless you add explicit machinery for that.

sections.title: How Services Discover Pods Whose IPs Change on Every Restart
sections.content:
Every Pod gets a unique IP address, but that IP is ephemeral — it changes on every restart, reschedule, or scale event. If your order-service hardcoded the IP of payment-service, it would break the moment Kubernetes moved the payment Pod to a different node.

**Services solve this with label selectors.** A Service definition says: route traffic to any Pod carrying the label `app: payment-service`. Kubernetes maintains an Endpoints object that lists the current IPs of all matching healthy Pods, updated in real time as Pods come and go. Other services call the Service's DNS name — `payment-service.namespace.svc.cluster.local` — which resolves to a stable virtual IP. Kube-proxy on each node translates that virtual IP into an actual Pod IP using iptables or IPVS rules.

The most common misconfiguration is a **label mismatch** between the Service's `spec.selector` and the Pod template's labels. The Service finds zero endpoints, and every request gets a connection refused error. Running `kubectl get endpoints <service-name>` immediately reveals whether any Pods are backing the Service — an empty list means the labels do not match.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Pod wraps containers, not equals container** — a Pod is one or more containers sharing network and storage; two containers in the same Pod communicate over localhost, not over the cluster network
- **Deployment controller runs a continuous reconciliation loop** — it compares desired state with actual state every few seconds and replaces crashed Pods automatically without any human intervention or alert
- **ReplicaSet is the hidden middle layer** — Deployments do not manage Pods directly; they create ReplicaSets, and rolling updates work by scaling up a new ReplicaSet while scaling down the old one
- **Services use label selectors, not hardcoded IPs** — the `spec.selector` matches Pod labels dynamically; a label mismatch produces zero endpoints and silent connection refused errors visible via `kubectl get endpoints`
- **ConfigMap updates do not restart Pods** — changing a ConfigMap value does not propagate to running containers unless you trigger a rolling restart or use Spring Cloud Kubernetes for live reload

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
In Kubernetes you never manage individual containers directly — you work with abstractions that the control plane continuously reconciles toward your declared desired state. The four you interact with constantly are Pod, Deployment, Service, and ConfigMap, and they form a hierarchy: Deployments manage ReplicaSets which manage Pods, Services route traffic to Pods by label selector, and ConfigMaps inject configuration at startup.

**Pod — the smallest deployable unit**
- A Pod wraps one or more containers that share a network namespace and storage volumes — they communicate over localhost and share the same IP address; you never create Pods directly in production for this reason
- Pods are ephemeral by design: when a node fails or a Pod is deleted, it is gone; the Deployment controller creates a replacement Pod, typically with a new IP — nothing should depend on a Pod's IP address directly
- The Pod spec sets resource requests and limits, liveness/readiness probes, environment variables, and volume mounts — all the container-level configuration lives here, not in the Deployment

**Deployment — the controller that keeps Pods running**
- A Deployment declares desired state: "run 3 replicas of `payment-service:v2.1`" — the controller loops continuously comparing actual versus desired state and creates or deletes Pods to close any gap
- Under the hood, Deployments manage ReplicaSets — when you update the image tag, the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and scales it up while scaling down the old one; this two-layer design enables zero-downtime rolling updates without additional tooling
- `kubectl rollout undo deployment/payment-service` reverts to the previous ReplicaSet in seconds — Kubernetes keeps a configurable revision history (default 10) specifically for this

**Service — stable network identity for ephemeral Pods**
- Pods get new IPs on every restart, so nothing should route to a Pod IP directly; a Service creates a stable virtual IP (ClusterIP) and DNS name — `payment-service.default.svc.cluster.local` — that survives Pod restarts
- The Service uses a label selector to find its target Pods — any Pod with matching labels receives traffic; `kubectl get endpoints payment-service` shows which Pod IPs are currently behind the selector
- Ingress sits in front of Services to terminate TLS and route HTTP traffic by path or hostname to different backend Services — the Service itself handles TCP load balancing, not HTTP-layer routing

questions.question: What is the difference between liveness, readiness, and startup probes in Kubernetes for Spring Boot?
questions.title: Kubernetes Probes: Liveness vs Readiness vs Startup for Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Liveness probe: is the container alive? Failure → Kubernetes restarts the pod. Readiness probe: is the container ready to serve traffic? Failure → Kubernetes removes the pod from Service endpoints (no restart). Startup probe: is the container still starting? Disables liveness/readiness until it passes, preventing restarts during slow JVM startup.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the different failure behaviors and when each probe type is needed
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not configuring a startup probe for Spring Boot — long JVM startup triggers liveness probe failures, causing restart loops before the app is ready
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain Spring Boot Actuator's /actuator/health/liveness and /health/readiness endpoints, discuss the restart loop scenario without startup probes, and mention setting failureThreshold appropriately

sections.title: The Restart Loop That Kills Every Spring Boot Deploy Without a Startup Probe
sections.content:
Picture this: your Spring Boot application takes 45 seconds to initialize — loading the Spring context, running Flyway migrations, warming caches. You deploy it to Kubernetes with a liveness probe set to check every 10 seconds after a 30-second delay. The probe fires at second 30, the app is not ready, the probe fails three times, and Kubernetes restarts the container. The new container starts initializing and the cycle repeats forever. Your deployment never completes.

This **restart loop** is the single most common Kubernetes failure for Spring Boot teams, and it exists because of a fundamental confusion between three probe types that look similar but trigger completely different behaviors. Liveness, readiness, and startup probes each answer a different question about the container's health, and each produces a different failure action. Mixing them up — or omitting the startup probe entirely — leads to either services that restart during normal startup or services that receive traffic before they can handle it.

The startup probe was added to Kubernetes specifically to solve this problem. It acts as a guard that holds off liveness and readiness checking until the application signals it has finished initializing. Without it, you are left guessing `initialDelaySeconds` — and guessing wrong means either restart loops or delayed detection of genuinely stuck pods.

sections.title: Three Questions With Three Different Consequences
sections.content:
The distinction between these probes is not the mechanism — all three can use HTTP, TCP, or exec checks. The distinction is what Kubernetes does when the probe fails.

| Probe | Question It Answers | On Failure | On Success |
|---|---|---|---|
| Liveness | Is the process stuck or deadlocked? | Restart the container | No action |
| Readiness | Can this pod handle requests right now? | Remove from Service endpoints | Add to Service endpoints |
| Startup | Has the application finished initializing? | Keep waiting (or restart after threshold) | Enable liveness and readiness |

**Liveness** should detect unrecoverable states — infinite loops, deadlocks, memory corruption. It should never check external dependencies like databases, because a temporary database outage would restart every pod simultaneously, turning a partial outage into a total one. **Readiness** is the right probe for dependency health: when the database connection pool is exhausted, readiness fails, the pod stops receiving traffic, and when the pool recovers, readiness passes again — all without a restart.

The **startup probe** runs exclusively during initialization and disables both liveness and readiness until it succeeds. You configure it with `failureThreshold` multiplied by `periodSeconds` equal to the maximum time your application might need to start. Once it passes, it never runs again for that pod's lifetime.

sections.title: Mapping Spring Boot Actuator Endpoints to Kubernetes Probe Configuration
sections.content:
Spring Boot 2.3+ provides dedicated probe endpoints that align perfectly with Kubernetes health checks. The `/actuator/health/liveness` endpoint reports the application's liveness state — it only fails if the application explicitly marks itself as broken via `LivenessState.BROKEN`. The `/actuator/health/readiness` endpoint reports readiness and fails when Spring detects unavailable dependencies.

The probe configuration in your Deployment spec maps directly to these endpoints. The sizing decision that matters is the startup probe's failure window, calculated as `failureThreshold` multiplied by `periodSeconds`.

```yaml
startupProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /actuator/health/liveness
    port: 8080
  failureThreshold: 30
  periodSeconds: 10
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /actuator/health/liveness
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /actuator/health/readiness
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3
```

This gives the application a **300-second startup window** (30 times 10). Once the startup probe succeeds, liveness checks every 10 seconds and triggers a restart after 3 consecutive failures — 30 seconds of being stuck. Readiness checks every 5 seconds, removing the pod from load balancing after 15 seconds of unhealthy dependencies. Notice `initialDelaySeconds` is absent because the startup probe makes it unnecessary — this approach adapts to varying startup times instead of hardcoding a guess. Enable these endpoints in `application.yml` by setting `management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled: true`, though Spring Boot 3.x activates them automatically when it detects a Kubernetes environment.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Liveness failure restarts, readiness failure removes from load balancer** — mixing these up causes either unnecessary restarts during database blips or continued traffic to pods that cannot serve requests
- **Startup probe prevents the restart loop** — without it, a Spring Boot app taking 45 seconds to start gets killed by a liveness probe set at 30 seconds, creating an infinite restart cycle that blocks deployment
- **Never put dependency checks in liveness** — a database blip failing liveness restarts every pod simultaneously, converting a partial downstream outage into a complete cluster-wide outage
- **`failureThreshold x periodSeconds` = startup window** — set this to your maximum boot time (e.g., 30 x 10s = 300s) instead of guessing `initialDelaySeconds` on the liveness probe
- **Spring Boot Actuator splits `/health/liveness` from `/health/readiness`** — liveness only fails when the app marks itself `BROKEN`; readiness fails and recovers automatically with dependency availability

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Kubernetes uses three probe types to determine container health, and they exist for different failure modes. Misconfiguring them — particularly confusing liveness with readiness — causes either cascading restarts that bring down a healthy application or traffic being sent to containers that are not ready.

**Liveness — is the JVM responding?**
- A failed liveness check causes Kubernetes to restart the container — it is the circuit breaker for deadlocked, hung, or permanently broken processes that cannot recover without a restart
- Use the Actuator liveness endpoint: `GET /actuator/health/liveness` — Spring Boot 2.3+ reports `UP` when the application context is healthy and not in a broken state; it does not check database connectivity, because a database outage should not restart healthy Pods
- Set a generous `initialDelaySeconds` (or use a startup probe) — a liveness probe that fires during Spring Boot's initialization period triggers a restart loop; the JVM appears unresponsive while loading application context

**Readiness — is the app ready for traffic?**
- A failed readiness check removes the Pod from the Service's endpoint list — traffic stops routing to it, but the Pod keeps running and can recover; this is the correct response to temporary overload or a slow downstream dependency
- Use the Actuator readiness endpoint: `GET /actuator/health/readiness` — Spring Boot's readiness state starts as `REFUSING_TRAFFIC` during initialization and transitions to `ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC` only after all ApplicationReadyEvent listeners complete, including database connection pool establishment
- Set readiness `failureThreshold` lower than liveness — readiness failing quickly removes a Pod from rotation; liveness requires more failures before triggering a restart to avoid restarting a slow-but-recovering Pod

**Startup — protecting slow-starting JVMs**
- A startup probe is the correct solution for slow Spring Boot applications; while it has not succeeded, liveness checks are disabled — this prevents restart loops during initialization
- `failureThreshold: 30` with `periodSeconds: 10` gives the application 5 minutes to start before Kubernetes considers it failed; after the startup probe succeeds, liveness and readiness take over with normal thresholds
- Without a startup probe, you must inflate `initialDelaySeconds` on the liveness probe — that delay also applies after real restarts, making recovery slower than necessary

questions.question: What are the differences between ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, and Ingress in Kubernetes?
questions.title: Kubernetes Service Types: ClusterIP vs NodePort vs LoadBalancer vs Ingress
questions.direct_answer: ClusterIP: internal-only cluster DNS, no external access (default). NodePort: exposes service on each node's IP + a static port. LoadBalancer: provisions a cloud load balancer with an external IP. Ingress: HTTP/HTTPS routing rules managed by an Ingress controller — the standard way to expose multiple services externally via a single load balancer.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Kubernetes networking and the progression from internal to external service exposure
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating a LoadBalancer service for every microservice — each provisions a separate cloud load balancer (expensive); use Ingress with ClusterIP services instead
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain Ingress controllers (nginx-ingress, AWS ALB), TLS termination at Ingress, and how path-based routing works to serve multiple services from one external IP

sections.title: The $500/Month Mistake: One LoadBalancer Per Microservice
sections.content:
A team running ten Spring Boot microservices on AWS creates a LoadBalancer Service for each one. Every `type: LoadBalancer` provisions a separate AWS Network Load Balancer — at roughly $16/month each plus data transfer costs, that is $160/month in infrastructure that serves no purpose. The correct architecture uses a single Ingress controller backed by one load balancer, with all ten services behind ClusterIP.

This mistake reveals a misunderstanding of the **Kubernetes service type hierarchy**. The four types — ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, and Ingress — form a progression from internal-only to external exposure. Each higher level builds on the one below it: a LoadBalancer automatically creates a NodePort, which automatically creates a ClusterIP. Understanding this layering prevents both over-exposure (making internal services externally reachable) and over-spending (provisioning unnecessary cloud resources).

For Java backend architectures, the decision is almost always simple. Internal microservice-to-microservice traffic uses ClusterIP exclusively — these services have no business being reachable from outside the cluster. External traffic enters through a single Ingress controller that routes by host or path to the appropriate internal ClusterIP Service. The only time you need a standalone LoadBalancer Service is for non-HTTP protocols like gRPC or raw TCP that Ingress controllers do not handle natively.

sections.title: From Internal to External: What Each Type Actually Does
sections.content:
Each service type provides a different level of network accessibility, and the cost and complexity increase at each level.

| Type | Reachable From | Mechanism | Cloud Cost | Best For |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ClusterIP | Inside cluster only | Virtual IP + DNS | None | Service-to-service calls |
| NodePort | Node IP + high port (30000-32767) | Opens port on every node | None | Dev/testing, bare-metal clusters |
| LoadBalancer | External IP | Cloud-provisioned LB (ALB, NLB) | ~$16+/month each | Single non-HTTP service needing external access |
| Ingress | External via HTTP/HTTPS | Ingress controller + routing rules | One LB shared across all services | Multiple HTTP services, TLS termination, path routing |

**NodePort** deserves special mention because it is rarely the right choice in cloud environments. It exposes your service on every node's IP at a high port — workable for local development with Minikube but operationally painful in production where you would need to manage node IP discovery, health checking, and firewall rules yourself.

**Ingress is not a Service type** — it is a separate Kubernetes resource that defines HTTP routing rules. An Ingress controller (NGINX, Traefik, or the AWS ALB Ingress Controller) watches these rules and configures its own load balancer accordingly. One Ingress controller handles routing for every external-facing service in the cluster.

sections.title: The Production Pattern: Ingress Plus ClusterIP for Everything Else
sections.content:
In a production Spring Boot microservices architecture, the networking pattern is consistent. Every service runs as ClusterIP, and a single Ingress controller manages external access.

Internal **east-west traffic** between services uses ClusterIP DNS names. When `order-service` calls `payment-service`, it resolves `payment-service.namespace.svc.cluster.local` to a virtual IP. Kube-proxy distributes requests across healthy pods using iptables or IPVS. No external networking is involved — traffic stays inside the cluster network with minimal latency.

External **north-south traffic** from users and API consumers enters through the Ingress controller. A typical Ingress resource routes different URL paths to different backend services.

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: api-ingress
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts: [api.example.com]
      secretName: tls-cert
  rules:
    - host: api.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /orders
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: {name: order-svc, port: {number: 80}}
          - path: /payments
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: {name: payment-svc, port: {number: 80}}
```

This single Ingress resource routes `/orders` to the order service and `/payments` to the payment service, all sharing one cloud load balancer. **TLS termination** happens at the Ingress level using a certificate stored in a Kubernetes Secret, so individual services do not need to handle HTTPS themselves. The cost saving compared to one LoadBalancer per service is significant — and the centralized TLS and routing configuration is operationally simpler.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **ClusterIP is the default and correct choice for internal traffic** — microservices call each other via DNS names like `payment-service.namespace.svc.cluster.local` without any external network exposure
- **One LoadBalancer per service is a costly anti-pattern** — each `type: LoadBalancer` provisions a separate cloud LB; ten services means ten LBs with ten monthly bills when one Ingress controller handles all of them
- **Ingress is not a Service type** — it is a separate Kubernetes resource defining HTTP routing rules processed by an Ingress controller (NGINX, Traefik, AWS ALB) that shares one load balancer across all services
- **TLS termination belongs at the Ingress layer** — store certificates as Kubernetes Secrets and configure them in the Ingress spec so individual services do not need to handle HTTPS or certificate management
- **NodePort is a development convenience, not a production solution** — it exposes services on high ports (30000-32767) across all nodes and requires external health checking and firewall management that Ingress handles automatically

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Kubernetes has four ways to expose a Service, and the choice determines both who can reach it and how traffic enters the cluster. Most teams never use NodePort in production; they use ClusterIP for internal services and a LoadBalancer-backed Ingress for external traffic.

**ClusterIP — internal cluster communication**
- ClusterIP is the default and creates a virtual IP reachable only from within the cluster — services talk to each other using this address; `payment-service.default.svc.cluster.local` resolves to the ClusterIP via CoreDNS
- This is the correct type for every service that should not be reachable from outside the cluster — databases, internal APIs, caches; using anything higher for these is a security exposure

**NodePort — fixed port on every node**
- NodePort opens a port (30000–32767) on every node's IP; traffic to `<any-node-ip>:<nodeport>` reaches the Service — useful for local development without a load balancer (like minikube) but exposes a high port on every node in production
- Production concerns: direct node IP exposure, the port range is inconvenient, and a node IP changes when the node restarts — NodePort is rarely appropriate for production external traffic

**LoadBalancer — cloud load balancer per service**
- `type: LoadBalancer` provisions a cloud load balancer per Service in platforms like AWS EKS, GKE, and AKS — traffic enters the cluster through the cloud load balancer's external IP
- The cost issue: one cloud load balancer per Service at $20–100/month each is expensive for a cluster with 20 Services — this is exactly the problem Ingress solves

**Ingress — one load balancer, many services**
- An Ingress resource defines HTTP(S) routing rules (path-based or host-based) to multiple backend Services behind a single cloud load balancer running the Ingress controller (nginx, AWS ALB, Traefik)
- Ingress handles TLS termination with certificates from cert-manager — the controller presents the correct certificate and routes decrypted traffic to the backend Service; individual Services remain ClusterIP
- The Ingress controller must be installed separately — `kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/...` installs the nginx controller; this is the piece developers most commonly forget when setting up a new cluster

sections.title: Three Missing Pieces That Separate a YAML File From a Production Deployment
sections.content:
Running `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml` is trivially easy. Getting that deployment to survive its first real incident is where most teams fail. The gap between a working deployment and a production-ready one comes down to three things that basic tutorials skip: **immutable image tags** so rollback actually works, **resource limits** so one pod cannot starve a node, and **health probes** so Kubernetes can distinguish a healthy pod from a crashing one.

Without immutable tags, `kubectl rollout undo` cannot guarantee you are reverting to the exact code that was running before — if the `latest` tag was overwritten in the registry, you are rolling forward to unknown code. Without resource limits, a memory leak in one pod triggers Linux OOM killer across the entire node, taking down co-located services. Without probes, Kubernetes has no signal to stop routing traffic to a pod that is starting up, deadlocked, or failing to connect to its database.

The deployment workflow itself is straightforward: build and tag an image, push to a registry, apply Kubernetes manifests. The production concerns live in the details of those manifests — how you configure the rolling update strategy, where you draw the line between requests and limits, and which probe types you configure for your Spring Boot application's specific startup characteristics.

sections.title: Why the Image Tag Determines Whether Rollback Works
sections.content:
The first step is building and pushing a Docker image with a **deterministic tag** — either the git commit SHA or a semantic version. The `latest` tag is the most dangerous shortcut in container deployment because it breaks two critical capabilities: rollback and audit.

When you run `kubectl rollout undo`, Kubernetes scales up the previous ReplicaSet which references the old image tag. If that tag was `latest` and someone has since pushed a new build to `latest`, the "rollback" pulls the newer image — you are not rolling back at all. With a SHA-based tag like `myapp:a1b2c3d`, the ReplicaSet pins to that exact build artifact.

The build step itself has two approaches. A `Dockerfile` gives you full control over the image contents but requires maintaining the file and understanding multi-stage builds for slim JVM images. **Jib** from Google builds optimized Docker images directly from Maven or Gradle without a Dockerfile — it layers dependencies, resources, and classes separately so that code changes produce small incremental layer pushes.

```bash
GIT_SHA=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
./mvnw jib:build -Dimage=myregistry.io/spring-app:${GIT_SHA}
```

This produces a properly layered image tagged with the exact commit that generated it. Every rollback, every audit, every incident investigation can trace a running pod back to a specific commit in version control.

sections.title: Resource Limits and Probes: What Kubernetes Needs From You to Manage Pods
sections.content:
A Deployment without resource limits or health probes is flying blind. Kubernetes uses **resource requests** for scheduling decisions — which node has room for this pod — and **limits** for runtime enforcement — kill the pod if it exceeds memory, throttle if it exceeds CPU. Without requests, the scheduler packs pods onto nodes randomly. Without limits, a single memory leak takes down every pod on the node.

For Spring Boot applications, the configuration needs to account for the JVM's memory model. Set memory requests to expected steady-state usage and limits with headroom for GC spikes. Use `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` so the JVM heap stays within the container's memory limit with room for metaspace, thread stacks, and code cache.

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: myregistry.io/spring-app:a1b2c3d
    resources:
      requests: {memory: 512Mi, cpu: 250m}
      limits:   {memory: 1Gi,   cpu: 1000m}
    startupProbe:
      httpGet: {path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080}
      failureThreshold: 30
      periodSeconds: 10
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet: {path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080}
      periodSeconds: 10
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet: {path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080}
      periodSeconds: 5
```

The **rolling update strategy** controls how Kubernetes transitions between versions. Setting `maxSurge: 1` and `maxUnavailable: 0` ensures zero downtime — Kubernetes creates one new pod, waits for it to pass readiness, then terminates one old pod, repeating until all pods are updated.

sections.title: From kubectl apply to Verified Zero-Downtime Rollout
sections.content:
With manifests ready, `kubectl apply -f k8s/` deploys all resources declaratively. The `-f` flag accepts a directory, applying every YAML file inside it. Track the rollout in real time with `kubectl rollout status deployment/spring-app` — this blocks until all pods in the new ReplicaSet are ready or the rollout fails.

If the new version fails readiness probes, the rollout stalls. Old pods remain running and serving traffic. At this point, you have two options: fix the issue and push a corrected image (which triggers a new rollout), or run `kubectl rollout undo deployment/spring-app` to immediately revert. The undo command scales up the previous ReplicaSet — because **Kubernetes retains old ReplicaSets** (controlled by `revisionHistoryLimit`, default 10), rollback is instant with no image rebuild.

For production deployments with **multiple environments**, use Kustomize or Helm to manage per-environment differences. Kustomize overlays patch base manifests with environment-specific values — different replica counts, different image tags, different resource limits. Helm charts template the same manifests with values files. Both approaches solve the same problem: avoiding copy-pasted YAML files that drift apart over time. The goal is one source of truth for the deployment shape, parameterized for dev, staging, and production.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Never use the `latest` image tag** — `kubectl rollout undo` with `latest` can pull a newer image instead of reverting, making rollback non-deterministic; always tag with commit SHA or semantic version
- **`maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0` guarantees zero downtime** — Kubernetes creates a replacement pod before terminating any existing one, so capacity never drops below the desired replica count during rollout
- **Resource limits prevent node-level collateral damage** — a pod without memory limits can trigger Linux OOM killer across the entire node, taking down every co-located service that was running fine
- **Startup probe eliminates `initialDelaySeconds` guessing** — set `failureThreshold x periodSeconds` to maximum boot time instead of hardcoding a delay that breaks when Flyway migrations run longer than expected
- **Kustomize or Helm for multi-environment deployments** — one set of base manifests parameterized per environment avoids copy-pasted YAML files that drift apart silently over weeks

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Deploying a Spring Boot application to Kubernetes involves five components working together: a containerized image, a Deployment, a Service, a ConfigMap, and an Ingress. Each element has one job, and the deploy process builds them in dependency order.

**Build and push the image**
- Tag the image with the registry path and a specific version: `docker build -t my-registry.io/payment-service:v1.2.3 .` then `docker push` — never use the `latest` tag in Kubernetes manifests because Kubernetes will not pull a new `latest` image if it already has a cached copy
- Authenticate to the registry from Kubernetes using an `imagePullSecret` — create it with `kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=...` and reference it in the Pod spec; missing this is the most common cause of `ErrImagePull`

**Deployment and ConfigMap**
- Write a Deployment YAML declaring the image, replica count, resource requests and limits, liveness/readiness probes, and environment variable references to ConfigMaps and Secrets — never hardcode configuration values in the Deployment spec
- Create the ConfigMap before the Deployment: `kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml && kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml` — a Deployment referencing a missing ConfigMap fails to create Pods with a `CreateContainerConfigError`
- Verify rollout completion: `kubectl rollout status deployment/payment-service` blocks until all replicas are running the new version or the rollout times out

**Service and Ingress**
- Create a ClusterIP Service with a label selector matching the Deployment's Pod labels — verify the selector works immediately with `kubectl get endpoints payment-service`; empty endpoints mean the selector does not match any running Pods
- Create the Ingress pointing to the Service by name — test the full path from outside the cluster with `curl -H "Host: payments.example.com" http://<ingress-ip>/api/payments` to confirm the entire routing chain is working before marking the deployment complete

questions.question: How do you manage configuration with ConfigMaps and Secrets for a Spring Boot application in Kubernetes?
questions.title: ConfigMaps and Secrets: Spring Boot Config Management in Kubernetes
questions.direct_answer: ConfigMaps store non-sensitive config injected as env vars or mounted as property files. Secrets store sensitive data (passwords, keys) with base64 encoding and RBAC access control. Spring Boot reads both via environment variables that override application.properties, or via volume mounts as property files. Never hardcode credentials — always use Secrets.

sections.title: The Gap Between 'Works Locally' and 'Works in Kubernetes': Configuration Injection
sections.content:
Every Spring Boot application carries configuration — database URLs, log levels, API keys, feature flags. Locally, these live in `application.properties` or `application.yml` files inside the JAR. In Kubernetes, the same application must run in dev, staging, and production from the same Docker image. **The image never changes; only the configuration changes.**

Kubernetes provides two primitives for external configuration: **ConfigMaps** for non-sensitive data and **Secrets** for credentials. Spring Boot's externalized configuration model makes this integration seamless — environment variables injected from ConfigMaps and Secrets override the values baked into `application.properties`, following Spring's property source precedence rules. No code changes, no conditional logic, no environment-specific builds.

The common trap is treating ConfigMaps and Secrets interchangeably. ConfigMaps are stored in plain text in etcd and are readable by anyone with namespace access. Secrets have separate RBAC policies and can be encrypted at rest when configured. Putting a database password in a ConfigMap means every developer with `kubectl get configmap` access can see it. The second trap is assuming that updating a ConfigMap automatically updates running pods — it does not, and this misunderstanding causes confused debugging sessions when config changes seem to have no effect.

sections.title: How Spring Boot's Relaxed Binding Eliminates Configuration Code Changes
sections.content:
Spring Boot's **relaxed binding** translates environment variable names to property paths automatically. The naming convention is mechanical: dots become underscores, everything is uppercase. `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` maps to `spring.datasource.url`. `MY_APP_MAX_CONNECTIONS` maps to `my.app.max-connections`. This means ConfigMap keys follow standard Kubernetes `SCREAMING_CASE` conventions without any adaptation code.

The injection mechanism in the Pod spec uses `envFrom` to load all keys from a ConfigMap or Secret as environment variables in one declaration.

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    envFrom:
      - configMapRef:
          name: spring-app-config
      - secretRef:
          name: spring-app-secrets
```

Every key in `spring-app-config` becomes an environment variable, and Spring Boot's property resolver picks them up at startup. The precedence order matters: environment variables override values in the packaged `application.properties`. This means the JAR carries sensible defaults for local development (`spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/myapp`), and the ConfigMap overrides them in Kubernetes (`SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://postgres-svc:5432/myapp`). Same image, different behavior, no rebuild required.

For complex configuration that does not fit flat key-value pairs, mount the ConfigMap as a file at `/config/application.yml`. Spring Boot automatically loads property files from this directory, making the full YAML structure available.

sections.title: Why Updating a ConfigMap Does Not Update Your Running Pods
sections.content:
This catches every team at least once: you update a ConfigMap with `kubectl apply`, verify the change with `kubectl get configmap`, and the running pods still use the old values. **Environment variables are set at container start and never re-read.** The ConfigMap update changed the source, but the environment was already injected into the running process.

There are three ways to handle this gap. The most common approach is triggering a **rolling restart** when the ConfigMap changes. Helm automates this with a checksum annotation in the Deployment's pod template — when the ConfigMap content changes, the checksum changes, the pod template hash changes, and Kubernetes rolls out new pods that pick up the updated values.

The second approach is **Spring Cloud Kubernetes Config**, which watches ConfigMap changes through the Kubernetes API and triggers a `@RefreshScope` reload on affected beans — no restart required. This works for Spring beans annotated with `@ConfigurationProperties` but does not work for values consumed during startup like database connection pool sizes.

The third approach is **volume-mounted ConfigMaps**, which the kubelet syncs approximately every 60 seconds. Applications that read configuration from disk files (not environment variables) can detect file changes and reload. Spring Boot's `spring.config.import=configtree:/config/` supports this pattern natively.

sections.title: Why Secrets Need More Than Base64 and What to Do About It
sections.content:
Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted. Run `kubectl get secret db-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d` and the password prints in plain text. Base64 is an encoding, not a security mechanism. The actual security layers are **RBAC** (controlling who can read Secrets in a namespace), **etcd encryption at rest** (encrypting Secret data in the cluster store), and **external secret managers**.

For production credentials, the strongest pattern is never storing the actual secret in Kubernetes at all. **External Secrets Operator** syncs secrets from AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, or GCP Secret Manager into Kubernetes Secrets automatically. Rotation happens in the external manager, and the operator propagates the new value. This gives you centralized audit logging, automatic rotation, and access policies that exist outside the Kubernetes RBAC boundary.

For teams not yet using an external secret manager, the minimum security baseline is encrypting etcd at rest (configured in the API server's `EncryptionConfiguration`) and restricting Secret access via RBAC Roles that explicitly deny `get` on Secrets to developers who do not need them. The `stringData` field in Secret manifests accepts plain text and auto-encodes to base64, which prevents manual encoding errors — but never commit Secret manifests with `stringData` values to version control.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Spring Boot relaxed binding maps `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` to `spring.datasource.url`** — no code changes needed; ConfigMap keys in SCREAMING_CASE automatically override packaged `application.properties` values at startup
- **`envFrom` injects all ConfigMap keys as env vars at once** — eliminates per-key `env` entries in the pod spec, but values are frozen at container creation and never re-read during the container's lifetime
- **ConfigMap updates do not restart pods** — environment variables are set once at container start; use Helm checksum annotations, Spring Cloud Kubernetes, or volume-mounted configs for live updates
- **Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted** — `kubectl get secret -o jsonpath | base64 -d` reveals credentials in plain text; enable etcd encryption at rest and restrict namespace-level RBAC access
- **External Secrets Operator pulls credentials from Vault or AWS Secrets Manager** — keeps actual secrets out of Kubernetes entirely, providing centralized rotation and audit logging outside the cluster boundary

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
ConfigMaps and Secrets both inject configuration into Pods, but they exist for different reasons: ConfigMaps are for non-sensitive configuration, Secrets are for credentials. The distinction matters because Kubernetes handles their access control and audit logging differently.

**ConfigMap — non-sensitive configuration**
- A ConfigMap stores key-value pairs or entire files; Spring Boot reads them as environment variables (`env.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef`) or as mounted property files (`spring.config.import=optional:configtree:/config/`)
- The configtree import mounts the ConfigMap as a directory where each key becomes a file; Spring Boot reads nested properties from file paths — `database.url` in the ConfigMap becomes `database.url` in the Spring environment
- Critical behavior: updating a ConfigMap does not restart running Pods — environment variables are frozen at container start; mounted files update eventually (within the kubelet sync period, ~60 seconds), but the application must watch for changes to pick them up; the safest approach is a rolling restart triggered by a Helm checksum annotation

**Secrets — credential injection**
- Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded by default, not encrypted — any user with `get secret` permission can read them; base64 is encoding, not security; enable etcd encryption-at-rest and RBAC restriction to make Secrets meaningful
- Spring Boot reads Secrets exactly like ConfigMaps — as environment variables or mounted files; prefer mounted files because environment variables appear in `kubectl describe pod` output and process listings
- In production, Kubernetes-native Secrets are often insufficient — use the External Secrets Operator to sync from AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, or GCP Secret Manager; the ESO fetches and rotates secrets without touching Kubernetes RBAC

**The environment variable reload problem**
- Neither ConfigMap nor Secret updates propagate to running containers as environment variables — the container must restart to see new values
- The Reloader controller (stakater/Reloader) watches for ConfigMap and Secret changes and triggers rolling restarts automatically — the standard solution for teams that need configuration updates without manual intervention
- Annotate the Deployment with `reloader.stakater.com/auto: "true"` and Reloader handles the rest; this pattern is safer than forcing teams to remember to trigger restarts after every config change

Set CPU requests to the typical CPU usage; set limits generously since CPU throttling (not OOMKill) slows GC. sections.title: The Silent Killer: Setting JVM Heap Equal to the Container Memory Limit
sections.content:
The most predictable OOMKill in Kubernetes: set your container memory limit to 1Gi, configure `-Xmx1g`, and watch the pod get killed within minutes. The JVM needs **more memory than just heap** — metaspace for loaded classes (100-200MB for a typical Spring Boot app), thread stacks (1MB per thread times 200+ threads), JIT code cache, garbage collector overhead, and NIO direct buffers. Setting `-Xmx` equal to the container limit leaves zero room for any of these, and the Linux cgroup kills the process the moment total resident memory exceeds the limit.

This is the single most common JVM-on-Kubernetes failure, and it stems from a mental model mismatch. In traditional deployments, the JVM was the only significant process on the machine and could negotiate with the OS for memory. In a container, the **cgroup memory limit is a hard ceiling** enforced by the kernel. There is no negotiation — exceed it by a single byte and the OOM killer terminates the process immediately.

The fix is straightforward: use `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` instead of a fixed `-Xmx`. This tells the JVM to use 75% of the container's available memory for heap, leaving 25% for non-heap allocations. For a 1Gi limit, heap maxes at roughly 768MB with approximately 256MB reserved for everything else.

sections.title: Memory Sizing: Why 75% Is the Right Heap-to-Container Ratio
sections.content:
The `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` flag works in conjunction with `-XX:+UseContainerSupport` (enabled by default since Java 10), which makes the JVM read cgroup memory limits instead of host memory. Together, they ensure the heap scales automatically with whatever memory limit you set on the container.

The 75% ratio is not arbitrary. A typical Spring Boot application's **non-heap breakdown** looks like this: metaspace consumes 100-200MB depending on the number of loaded classes (Spring's reflection-heavy model loads thousands), thread stacks at 1MB each add up with Tomcat's default 200-thread pool, code cache for JIT-compiled methods needs 50-100MB, and the garbage collector itself needs working memory for reference processing. The remaining 25% of a 1Gi limit (approximately 256MB) covers these allocations with a safety margin.

The Deployment manifest configures both the container limits and the JVM flags through the `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` environment variable.

```yaml
env:
  - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
    value: >-
      -XX:+UseContainerSupport
      -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0
      -XX:InitialRAMPercentage=50.0
resources:
  requests: {memory: 512Mi, cpu: 250m}
  limits:   {memory: 1Gi,   cpu: 1000m}
```

**Requests** determine scheduling — the scheduler ensures the node has 512Mi free before placing the pod. **Limits** determine enforcement — exceeding 1Gi triggers an OOMKill. The gap between requests and limits defines the QoS class: equal values produce `Guaranteed` (never evicted under pressure), unequal values produce `Burstable` (evicted before Guaranteed pods).

sections.title: CPU Throttling Damages Your P99 Latency Without Any Visible Error
sections.content:
Memory limit violations are dramatic — the container is killed and restarted with exit code 137. CPU limit violations are silent and insidious. When a container exceeds its CPU quota, the Linux CFS scheduler **pauses the entire cgroup** until the next scheduling period. The JVM stops — all threads frozen — and resumes when the quota refills.

This throttling manifests as latency spikes that are impossible to diagnose from application logs alone. The JVM does not know it was paused. Garbage collection that should take 20ms takes 200ms because the GC threads were frozen mid-cycle. A request that should complete in 5ms takes 50ms because the CPU quota was exhausted by a concurrent GC pause. Your P99 latency graph shows unexplained spikes while P50 looks normal.

The **`container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total`** Prometheus metric is the diagnostic key. If throttling exceeds 5% of total CPU time, either increase the CPU limit or remove it entirely. Many production teams remove CPU limits and keep only CPU requests — this gives `Burstable` QoS with the freedom to burst during GC pauses and JIT compilation without throttling. The trade-off is that a CPU-intensive pod could temporarily affect co-located pods, but the scheduler uses requests for placement decisions so resources are still reserved.

For latency-critical services where predictability matters more than flexibility, set requests equal to limits for `Guaranteed` QoS. The scheduler reserves exactly those resources, and the pod is last in line for eviction during node pressure.

sections.content:
- **`-Xmx` must never equal the container memory limit** — metaspace, thread stacks, code cache, and GC overhead need 200-400MB beyond heap; setting them equal guarantees OOMKill within hours of running
- **`MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` with `UseContainerSupport`** — JVM reads cgroup limits and sets heap to 75% of the container's memory, leaving 25% for non-heap allocations automatically
- **CPU throttling causes invisible latency spikes** — when the CPU quota is exhausted, Linux pauses the entire cgroup including GC threads; P99 spikes while P50 looks normal and no errors appear in logs
- **Requests drive scheduling, limits drive enforcement** — requests determine which node the pod lands on; memory limits trigger OOMKill, CPU limits trigger throttling without termination
- **QoS class determines eviction priority** — `requests == limits` gives Guaranteed (last evicted under node pressure); `requests < limits` gives Burstable; no requests at all gives BestEffort (first evicted)

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Kubernetes resource requests and limits are the two numbers the scheduler and kubelet use to decide where to place Pods and when to kill them. Getting them wrong for a JVM application is one of the most common causes of OOMKilled pods and degraded cluster scheduling.

**Requests — scheduling guarantees**
- `resources.requests` tells the scheduler how much CPU and memory this Pod needs — the scheduler places the Pod on a node that has at least this much available; if no node has enough, the Pod stays Pending
- Requests define the Pod's QoS class: if requests equal limits, the Pod gets Guaranteed QoS and is the last to be evicted under node memory pressure; if limits exceed requests (Burstable), the Pod can be evicted; no limits at all gives BestEffort QoS and the Pod is evicted first
- Set memory requests based on actual idle JVM footprint — `kubectl top pod` during normal operation; setting requests too low causes the scheduler to pack too many JVMs onto one node, leading to OOMKills when they all ramp up simultaneously

**Limits — enforcement ceilings**
- `resources.limits.memory` is a hard ceiling enforced by cgroups — if the container exceeds it, the kernel OOMKills the process; there is no warning and the JVM has no chance to clean up
- Set memory limits to at least 1.5x the heap (`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`) to account for Metaspace, thread stacks, and direct buffers — a JVM with 512 MB heap needs at least 700–800 MB total container limit
- CPU limits throttle the process using the cgroup CPU quota — a JVM hitting the CPU limit slows down but is not killed; excessive CPU throttling (visible in `container_cpu_throttled_seconds_total`) degrades GC performance because GC threads are also throttled

**Recommended settings**
- Set `requests.memory = limits.memory` for a Guaranteed QoS class — JVMs have unpredictable memory footprints and should not be in competition with other Pods for memory; predictable memory allocation is worth the loss of burst capacity
- Leave CPU limits unset or set them generously — CPU throttling on a JVM degrades latency under load without providing meaningful protection; use CPU requests for scheduling placement without CPU limits for execution

questions.question: How do rolling updates and rollbacks work in Kubernetes Deployments?
questions.title: Kubernetes Rolling Updates and Rollbacks
questions.direct_answer: Rolling updates replace pods incrementally — new pods start, pass readiness probes, then old pods are terminated. Controlled by maxSurge (extra pods during update) and maxUnavailable (pods allowed offline). Zero-downtime requires maxUnavailable=0. Rollback with kubectl rollout undo restores the previous ReplicaSet.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how Kubernetes achieves zero-downtime deployments
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not setting maxUnavailable=0 (allows pods to be taken down before replacements are ready), or not having readiness probes (new pods receive traffic before they're ready to serve it)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Kubernetes keeps the previous ReplicaSet for rollback, discuss revisionHistoryLimit, and mention blue-green vs canary as alternatives to rolling for risk reduction

sections.title: Why maxUnavailable=0 Is the Only Setting That Guarantees Zero Downtime
sections.content:
A rolling update sounds simple: replace old pods with new ones gradually. But the default settings do not guarantee zero downtime. The Kubernetes default is `maxSurge: 25%` and `maxUnavailable: 25%` — meaning Kubernetes can terminate 25% of your pods before replacements are ready. For a 4-replica Deployment, that is one pod killed before the new version is running. During that window, your service has reduced capacity and may drop requests if load is high.

**Zero downtime requires `maxUnavailable: 0`** explicitly. This tells Kubernetes to never terminate an old pod until a new one has started and passed its readiness probe. Combined with `maxSurge: 1`, the Deployment creates one extra pod running the new version, waits for it to become ready, then terminates one old pod. Capacity never drops below the desired count.

The mechanism that makes this work is the **ReplicaSet**. When you change a Deployment's pod template (usually the image tag), the Deployment controller creates a new ReplicaSet for the new version. Both ReplicaSets exist simultaneously during the transition — the new one scaling up, the old one scaling down. Kubernetes keeps the old ReplicaSet around (scaled to zero replicas) after the rollout completes, which is what makes instant rollback possible.

sections.title: The Rollout Dance: New ReplicaSet Scales Up While Old Keeps Serving
sections.content:
When you run `kubectl set image deployment/spring-app app=myapp:v2` or apply an updated manifest, the Deployment controller creates a new ReplicaSet specifying the v2 image and begins scaling it up.

With `maxSurge: 1` and `maxUnavailable: 0` on a 4-replica Deployment, the rollout proceeds in lock-step fashion.

```yaml
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxSurge: 1
    maxUnavailable: 0
```

The sequence unfolds one pod at a time: Kubernetes creates pod v2-1 (total pods: 4 old + 1 new = 5). It waits for v2-1 to pass its readiness probe. Once ready, it terminates one v1 pod (total: 3 old + 1 new = 4). Then it creates v2-2, waits for readiness, terminates another v1 pod, and repeats until all 4 pods run v2.

**Readiness probes are the quality gate.** If the new version fails its readiness probe — because of a startup crash, a bad database migration, or a misconfigured environment variable — the rollout stalls. The old pods continue serving traffic indefinitely. This is why readiness probes and `maxUnavailable: 0` work as a pair: together they guarantee that users never see an unavailable or unhealthy pod.

sections.title: Rollback Is Instant Because Kubernetes Never Throws Away the Old ReplicaSet
sections.content:
The most powerful aspect of Kubernetes rollback is what it does not do: rebuild images, re-download layers, or re-run CI pipelines. When you run `kubectl rollout undo deployment/spring-app`, Kubernetes simply scales the previous ReplicaSet back up and scales the current one down. The old pods' image references are still in the ReplicaSet spec — Kubernetes pulls the image (usually from cache) and starts pods immediately.

This works because the Deployment retains old ReplicaSets up to the **`revisionHistoryLimit`** (default: 10). Each ReplicaSet records the exact pod template that was used, including image tag, environment variables, and resource limits. Rolling back to revision 3 does not mean reconstructing what revision 3 looked like — it means scaling up the ReplicaSet that already has that specification.

The `kubectl rollout history deployment/spring-app` command shows available revisions with their change annotations. For more targeted rollbacks, `kubectl rollout undo --to-revision=3` lets you skip intermediate revisions. If the rollback itself fails readiness probes, the same protection applies — old pods keep serving while the system waits.

For scenarios where rolling updates are too risky — a database schema change that could break both old and new versions simultaneously — **blue-green deployment** is the alternative. Deploy the new version as a separate Deployment, verify it independently, then update the Service's label selector to switch traffic atomically. This eliminates the mixed-version window that rolling updates create.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`maxUnavailable: 0` is required for zero downtime** — the Kubernetes default of 25% allows pods to be terminated before replacements are ready, briefly reducing capacity below the desired replica count
- **Readiness probes gate the rollout** — if new pods fail readiness checks, the rollout stalls and old pods continue serving traffic indefinitely; without probes, bad deployments receive traffic immediately
- **Rollback reuses existing ReplicaSets** — `kubectl rollout undo` scales up the previous ReplicaSet without rebuilding images; old pod specs are retained up to `revisionHistoryLimit` (default 10)
- **`revisionHistoryLimit` controls rollback depth** — lower values save etcd storage but limit how far back you can revert; set to at least 5 for production Deployments running frequent releases
- **Blue-green avoids the mixed-version window** — deploy the new version as a separate Deployment and switch the Service selector atomically when validated, eliminating the period where old and new pods serve simultaneously

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Kubernetes rolling updates replace running Pods incrementally — new Pods start before old Pods terminate, maintaining availability throughout the deployment. The two parameters that control the update speed and risk are `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable`.

**Rolling update mechanics**
- `maxSurge: 1` allows one Pod above the desired replica count during rollout — with 3 replicas, Kubernetes starts one new Pod (4 total), waits for it to pass readiness, then terminates one old Pod; this continues until all Pods run the new version
- `maxUnavailable: 0` ensures zero Pod downtime — no old Pod terminates until its replacement passes the readiness probe; set this to 0 in production for services that cannot tolerate reduced capacity during deploys
- The readiness probe is the critical coupling: a broken new version where the readiness probe never passes causes the rollout to stall — old Pods keep serving traffic, the broken new Pod sits in `0/1 Running`, and the rollout never progresses; this is a feature, not a bug

**Triggering and monitoring**
- `kubectl set image deployment/payment-service app=payment-service:v2.1.0` triggers a rolling update — Kubernetes records this as a new revision in the rollout history
- `kubectl rollout status deployment/payment-service` blocks and streams progress until all replicas are on the new version or the `progressDeadlineSeconds` (default 600s) elapses
- `kubectl rollout history deployment/payment-service` shows the revision history; add `--record` to the apply command (deprecated but still useful) or use annotation-based change-cause recording

**Rollback**
- `kubectl rollout undo deployment/payment-service` reverts to the previous ReplicaSet immediately — the old Pods that were terminated are recreated from the previous ReplicaSet spec; no image rebuild required
- `kubectl rollout undo deployment/payment-service --to-revision=3` rolls back to a specific revision — useful when the last version is also broken and you need to skip back further
- The `revisionHistoryLimit` field (default 10) controls how many old ReplicaSets Kubernetes keeps; setting it too low means you cannot roll back past recent releases

questions.question: How do you configure Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for a Spring Boot service in Kubernetes?
questions.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) for Spring Boot Services
questions.direct_answer: HPA automatically scales pod replicas based on CPU utilization, memory usage, or custom metrics. Requires resource requests set on the container. Configure with kubectl autoscale or a HPA YAML resource. For Spring Boot, expose custom metrics via Micrometer and Prometheus Adapter for traffic-based scaling (requests per second) rather than just CPU.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Kubernetes auto-scaling and its prerequisites (resource requests, metrics server)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not setting resource requests — HPA can't calculate CPU utilization percentage without a defined request baseline
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the metrics pipeline (Metrics Server for CPU/memory, Prometheus Adapter for custom metrics), discuss scale-down stabilization to prevent flapping, and mention KEDA for event-driven autoscaling

sections.title: Why CPU-Based Scaling Misleads You About Spring Boot Traffic Load
sections.content:
The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler's default metric — CPU utilization — works well for CPU-bound workloads like image processing or scientific computing. For a typical Spring Boot REST service, CPU tells you almost nothing about actual load. A service handling 500 requests per second might sit at 20% CPU because most of the latency is I/O wait on database calls. HPA sees low CPU, keeps the replica count low, and the service drowns in queued requests while CPU looks idle.

The fundamental problem is that **HPA calculates CPU utilization as a percentage of the resource request**. If you request 250m CPU and the pod uses 175m, HPA sees 70% utilization — regardless of whether the pod is handling 10 requests or 10,000. Without resource requests defined at all, HPA has no denominator for the calculation and simply cannot function. This is the prerequisite that most setup guides mention once and teams forget until they wonder why their pods never scale.

Custom metrics — requests per second, response latency, queue depth — give HPA semantically meaningful inputs. Instead of asking "is this pod using a lot of CPU?" you ask "is this pod handling more requests than it should?" The metrics pipeline involves Spring Boot Micrometer exposing metrics, Prometheus scraping them, and Prometheus Adapter translating them into the Kubernetes custom metrics API that HPA queries.

sections.title: The Prerequisite Everyone Forgets: Resource Requests Are the Denominator
sections.content:
HPA's CPU-based scaling formula is `current CPU usage / CPU request x 100`. Without a **CPU request** defined on the container, this formula has no denominator and HPA reports `<unknown>` for the target. The pods never scale up, even under massive load. Setting `resources.requests.cpu: 250m` gives HPA the baseline it needs.

The target utilization percentage — typically 70% — determines the scaling threshold. HPA continuously calculates the desired replica count: `desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas x currentUtilization / targetUtilization)`. If 3 pods average 90% CPU utilization with a 70% target, HPA computes `ceil(3 x 90/70)` = 4 replicas and scales up.

The **`minReplicas` and `maxReplicas`** fields bound the scaling range. Always set `minReplicas` to at least 2 for availability — a single pod during a scale-down means a restart takes your service completely offline. Set `maxReplicas` to cap costs and prevent runaway scaling from feedback loops. The HPA configuration declares these constraints alongside the target metric.

```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: spring-app
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
```

This HPA watches the `spring-app` Deployment and adjusts replicas between 2 and 20 to maintain approximately 70% average CPU utilization across all pods.

sections.title: Custom Metrics From Micrometer Give You Meaningful Scaling Triggers
Stabilization Windows Prevent the Scale-Down Flapping Loop
sections.content:
Without stabilization, HPA reacts to momentary metric changes. A brief traffic dip causes HPA to scale down, then traffic returns and HPA scales back up. Each scale-down terminates pods, losing their warm JVM caches and connection pools. Each scale-up starts cold pods that take 30+ seconds to initialize. This **flapping** wastes resources and degrades latency during every cycle.

The `behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds` field solves this by requiring the metric to stay below the threshold for a sustained period before HPA removes replicas. A 300-second window (5 minutes) means HPA only scales down if average utilization has been below the target continuously for 5 minutes.

```yaml
behavior:
  scaleDown:
    stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
    policies:
      - type: Pods
        value: 1
        periodSeconds: 60
  scaleUp:
    stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
    policies:
      - type: Percent
        value: 100
        periodSeconds: 15
```

Scale-up is configured aggressively — no stabilization delay, doubling capacity every 15 seconds if needed. Scale-down is conservative — wait 5 minutes, then remove only 1 pod per minute. This **asymmetric behavior** matches the cost profile of scaling decisions: adding capacity is cheap and fast, but removing capacity prematurely costs you cache warmth and startup latency. In practice, 5 minutes of scale-down stabilization eliminates almost all flapping without noticeably increasing cost.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Resource requests are HPA's denominator** — without CPU requests defined, HPA reports `<unknown>` and never scales; this is the most common misconfiguration that blocks autoscaling entirely
- **CPU utilization misleads for I/O-bound Spring Boot services** — a service at 20% CPU may be drowning in queued requests because latency is dominated by database I/O, not computation
- **Custom metrics via Micrometer and Prometheus Adapter** — enables HPA to scale on requests per second or queue depth instead of CPU, giving semantically meaningful scaling triggers tied to actual load
- **Scale-down stabilization prevents flapping** — `stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300` requires 5 minutes of sustained low utilization before removing pods, avoiding wasteful cycles that lose warm JVM caches
- **KEDA scales from zero for event-driven workloads** — Kafka consumers and SQS processors benefit from queue-depth-based scaling that HPA cannot provide since HPA requires `minReplicas` of at least 1

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler watches a metric and adjusts the replica count to keep that metric near a target value. For Spring Boot APIs, CPU utilization is the standard starting point — when CPU climbs above the target, HPA adds replicas; when it drops, HPA removes them.

**How HPA calculates scaling**
- HPA divides the current metric value by the target: if target CPU is 50% and actual average CPU is 80%, the scaling factor is 80/50 = 1.6 — applied to 3 replicas this yields a desired 5 replicas (3 × 1.6, rounded up)
- The metric server must be installed in the cluster for CPU and memory HPA to work — `kubectl top pods` working confirms the metrics pipeline is functional; HPA that shows `<unknown>` for current value means the metrics server is missing or misconfigured
- HPA respects `minReplicas` and `maxReplicas` as hard bounds — it will never scale below or above these values regardless of what the metric says; set `minReplicas` high enough to handle sudden traffic spikes before autoscaling has time to react

**Scaling down cooldown**
- HPA scales up aggressively (within 15 seconds of metric crossing threshold) but scales down conservatively — by default it waits 5 minutes after the last scale-down decision before reducing replicas further; this prevents flapping under variable load
- Adjust with `behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds` — reduce it for stateless services that are cheap to restart; leave it longer for services with slow startup or warm-up costs
- Scale-down removes the replica count from the Deployment but the actual Pod termination follows the `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` — ensure Spring Boot's graceful shutdown is configured so in-flight requests complete before the Pod dies

**Custom metrics with KEDA**
- KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) scales on application-specific metrics: Kafka consumer lag, queue depth, RabbitMQ message count — better signals than CPU for I/O-bound Spring Boot consumers
- A Kafka consumer whose consumer group lag is 10,000 messages needs more replicas even if CPU is at 5%; CPU-based HPA would never trigger; KEDA's Kafka scaler responds to the lag metric directly
- KEDA installs as a custom controller and defines `ScaledObject` resources that reference your Deployment — it replaces the standard HPA for KEDA-managed targets
